items.availability_note: Folic acid (pteroylmonoglutamic acid) is a manufactured molecule that does not occur in natural food. It is made by chemical synthesis (Waller condensation of a triaminopyrimidinone with a three-carbon unit and p-aminobenzoyl-L-glutamic acid) and is fully oxidised with a single glutamate. Natural foods contain reduced folate polyglutamates, chiefly 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, which is a different compound with different handling. The only folic acid in the food supply is what fortification put there, so the foods listed below are fortified products carrying analytically measured folic acid (USDA reports 'folic acid' and 'folate, food' as separate components). Rich natural food-folate sources exist and are listed with numbers in the dose_gap field, but they supply food folate, not folic acid.

items.dose_gap: DFE arithmetic first: 1 ug food folate = 1 ug DFE, 1 ug folic acid in a fortified food = 1.7 ug DFE, and folic acid taken fasting = 2.0 ug DFE (the 1.7 multiplier comes from assuming 85% availability for folic acid against 50% for food folate; Suitor and Bailey, PMID 10646010). So the standard 400 ug/day periconceptional folic acid tablet is worth about 680 ug DFE with food, 800 ug DFE fasting. Matching 680 ug DFE from natural food folate, per day, every day: 376 g cooked lentils (1.9 cups; 181 ug DFE/100 g, 358 ug per 198 g cup, FDC 172421), or 219 g prepared edamame (1.4 cups; 311 ug/100 g, 482 ug per 155 g cup, FDC 168411), or 269 g braised beef liver (253 ug/100 g, 172 ug per 68 g slice, FDC 168626), or 395 g cooked chickpeas (172 ug/100 g, 282 ug per 164 g cup, FDC 173757), or roughly 351 g raw spinach, about twelve 30 g cups (194 ug/100 g, FDC 168462), or 456 g cooked asparagus, about thirty spears (149 ug/100 g, 89 ug per 4-spear 60 g portion, FDC 168390), or 630 g boiled broccoli (108 ug/100 g, 84 ug per 78 g half-cup, FDC 169967). Technically reachable, practically not sustained. The UK high-risk dose of 5 mg/day is 8,500 ug DFE, about 4.7 kg of cooked lentils a day: unreachable by any diet. And the quantitative gap is not the main problem. Cuskelly, McNulty and Scott randomised 62 women to an extra 400 ug/day as a folic acid supplement, as folic-acid-fortified food, as natural food folate, or as dietary advice: red cell folate rose only in the supplement and fortified-food arms, and did not change in the food-folate arms despite documented increases in intake (Lancet 1996;347:657-9, PMID 8596381). The two trials that established the effect used synthetic folic acid: 4 mg/day (MRC Vitamin Study, Lancet 1991;338:131-7, PMID 1677062) and 0.8 mg/day in a multivitamin (Czeizel and Dudas, N Engl J Med 1992;327:1832-5, PMID 1307234). No trial has shown that food folate prevents neural tube defects. Telling a woman planning pregnancy to eat leafy greens instead of taking the tablet is not a conservative substitution, it is an untested one.
items.form_caveat: Folic acid is not bioidentical to food folate and the difference cuts both ways. It must be reduced by dihydrofolate reductase before it can enter one-carbon metabolism, and human DHFR capacity is low: unmetabolised folic acid appears in serum above a threshold of about 266 ug of folic acid per meal (Kelly et al., Am J Clin Nutr 1997;65:1790-5, PMID 9174474), which a 400 ug tablet exceeds. That is why the adult UL is set at 1,000 ug/day of folic acid from supplements and fortified food, with no UL on food folate: high folic acid can correct the megaloblastic anaemia of B12 deficiency while the neurological damage continues, so it masks the diagnosis. The concentrated-extract concern runs the other way here. Food folate has no toxicity ceiling; the synthetic form does. Separately, L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate (calcium methylfolate) supplements are marketed as the 'natural' or 'MTHFR-friendly' alternative, but no periconceptional trial has been run on them and the DFE conversion factors for them were only formally derived later (EFSA, PMC9399872); the neural-tube-defect evidence base is specifically folic acid (Czeizel, Ann Nutr Metab 2011, PMID 21865678).
items.bioavailability: Food folate is roughly 50% available against about 85% for folic acid eaten with food and close to 100% fasting; a long-term controlled feeding study in young women found food folate about 60% as effective as added folic acid in a mixed diet, supporting the 1.7 multiplier. Food folate is a polyglutamate that must be deconjugated at the brush border before absorption, and it is chemically fragile. USDA Table of Nutrient Retention Factors, Release 6 (2007) gives folate retention of 45% for legumes boiled 45-75 min and drained (retention code 0521), 30% for legumes boiled 2-2.5 h (code 0541), 60% for greens boiled in water to cover and drained (code 3005), and 90% for potatoes baked in the skin (code 3301). A cup of dried lentils simmered for an hour loses over half its folate, and the composition table value describes the cooked food only if the cooking matches. Folic acid in a fortified food or a tablet is stable and its dose is what the label says.

items.availability_note: Rich in animal foods and effectively absent from plant foods. Cobalamin is synthesised only by bacteria and archaea; plants have no pathway for it and no requirement for it. Every reliable dietary source is an animal that accumulated bacterial B12, or a bacterially fermented or fortified product. On the four contested claims: SPIRULINA IS NOT USABLE. Watanabe et al. showed that 83% of the cobamide in spirulina tablets is pseudovitamin B12 (adeninylcobamide), which is inactive in humans, and only 17% is real B12 (J Agric Food Chem 1999;47:4736-41, PMID 10552882, DOI 10.1021/jf990541b). Microbiological assays cannot distinguish the two, which is why spirulina labels claim high B12. Pseudovitamin B12 can also compete with the real thing. NORI IS USABLE, and is the only credible plant source: dried purple laver contains five biologically active cobalamin forms, with coenzyme forms (adenosyl- and methylcobalamin) about 60% of the total, and it corrected B12 status in deficient rats (PMID 11430774). Reported contents range from 32.3 ug/100 g dry weight (Japanese Porphyra) to 133.8 ug/100 g (Korean purple laver), with 51.7 ug/100 g for seasoned toasted Korean laver (Watanabe et al., Nutrients 2014;6:1861-73, PMID 24803097). TEMPEH IS NOT RELIABLE: 0.7-8.0 ug/100 g, entirely dependent on which bacteria happened to contaminate the Rhizopus fermentation, so a given batch may contain none. MUSHROOMS ARE NOT USABLE: dried shiitake averages 5.61 ug/100 g dry weight (range 1.3-12.7), black trumpet and golden chanterelle 1.09-2.65 ug/100 g dry weight, and most other species about 0.09 ug/100 g or trace; lion's mane contains the inactive B12[c-lactone] analogue. Chlorella varies from zero to several hundred ug/100 g between products and cannot be relied on. Kimchi and fermented vegetables are below 0.1 ug/100 g.

items.dose_gap: Two different gaps, and conflating them is the usual error. Against the 2.4 ug/day RDA there is no gap at all for anyone eating animal food: a single 3 oz portion of cooked clams supplies 35 times the RDA, a slice of liver 20 times, a can of sardines 3.4 times. Against the supplement dose there is an unbridgeable gap. Oral B12 supplements are typically 500-1,000 ug, and 1,000-2,000 ug for treating deficiency. To have 1,000 ug of B12 physically present in a meal you would need 1.01 kg of cooked clams, or 1.42 kg of braised beef liver, or 11.2 kg of canned sardines, or 35.7 kg of cooked salmon, or 222 litres of whole milk. That is the wrong comparison anyway: intrinsic-factor-mediated absorption saturates at about 1.5-2.0 ug per meal (Watanabe, Exp Biol Med 2007;232:1266-74, PMID 17959839, DOI 10.3181/0703-mr-67), so everything above roughly 2 ug in any single sitting is absorbed only by passive diffusion at on the order of 1%. A 1,000 ug tablet works precisely because 1% of 1,000 ug bypasses the receptor route. No food can deliver that, and no food needs to unless the receptor route is broken. For a strict vegan the picture inverts: no food reliably supplies even the 2.4 ug RDA except dried nori, and Watanabe puts the requirement at about 4 g/day of dried purple laver, which is roughly one and a half sheets eaten every day of a product whose content varies fourfold by origin and degrades with toasting and storage. That is a thin thread to hang a neurological outcome on. Fortified foods or a tablet are the honest answer.
items.form_caveat: Supplements use cyanocobalamin, which is not a form found in food; the cyanide ligand is a manufacturing artefact of the purification step and is removed intracellularly. Food B12 is protein-bound and needs gastric acid and pepsin to release it before intrinsic factor can take it up, so proton pump inhibitors, atrophic gastritis, gastric surgery and metformin knock out food B12 while leaving free crystalline B12 in a tablet or fortified cereal largely usable. This is the one case in this set where the supplement is the correct choice on mechanism, not just convenience. The dangerous form issue is the reverse of the usual concentration worry: algae supplements are not too strong, they are inactive. A spirulina capsule labelled as a B12 source delivers mostly pseudovitamin B12, and the assay that generated the label number could not tell the difference. Note also that the USDA figure for yeast extract spread is only 0.50 ug B12/100 g (FDC ID 167717), which is 0.03 ug per 6 g teaspoon: yeast itself does not make B12, so any yeast product that is a real B12 source is fortified, and the number belongs to the fortification, not the yeast.
items.bioavailability: About 50% of dietary B12 is assumed absorbed from a normal meal, but it varies sharply by food: fish 42%, sheep meat 56-89%, chicken 61-66%, and eggs under 9% (Watanabe 2007, PMID 17959839). The last figure matters because eggs are routinely offered to vegetarians as a B12 food; on absorbed B12 a large egg delivers well under 0.05 ug, which is under 2% of the RDA rather than the 19% the content figure implies. Cooking costs real B12 too. USDA Table of Nutrient Retention Factors Release 6 (2007) gives B12 retention of 70% for roasted beef (code 1301 group), 60% for beef braised or simmered without the drippings, 65% for roasted chicken, 60% for liver simmered without drippings, 90% for baked lean finfish, 60% for shellfish boiled in the shell against 90% steamed, and only 30% for milk held at heat for an hour. Keeping the pan juices recovers much of it, which is why the with-drippings factors run 15 points higher.

items.availability_note: Vitamin B6 itself is abundant and widely distributed: fish, organ meat, poultry, potatoes, bananas, pistachios and fortified cereals all carry useful amounts, and dietary deficiency is uncommon in people eating normally. The high-dose supplement is a different object. It is pyridoxine hydrochloride, a manufactured crystalline salt, sold at 50, 100 and sometimes 250-500 mg per tablet, which is 40 to 400 times the 1.3 mg adult RDA. Food is a rich source of the vitamin and not a source of the dose.

items.dose_gap: A 100 mg pyridoxine tablet is 77 times the RDA. Matching it by eating, in one day: 8.93 kg of pistachios, or 9.80 kg of braised beef liver, or 10.7 kg of raw yellowfin tuna, or 16.7 kg of roasted chicken breast, or 27.2 kg of banana, which is about 231 medium bananas. A 50 mg tablet still needs 4.5 kg of pistachios or 116 bananas. Even the regulatory ceiling is out of dietary reach: EFSA's 2023 tolerable upper intake level of 12 mg/day for adults corresponds to about 1.07 kg of pistachios or 3.27 kg of banana, roughly 28 bananas, every day. Ordinary diets deliver a few mg per day, an order of magnitude below the UL and two to three orders below the supplement. This is the mechanical reason for the requested point: dietary B6 has never produced the sensory neuropathy that supplements produce, because no food is concentrated enough to get near the toxic range. The syndrome was first described at 2-6 g/day of pyridoxine (Schaumburg et al., N Engl J Med 1983, PMID 6308447), cases have since been reported at far lower supplemental doses, and EFSA cut the adult UL from the SCF's 25 mg/day to 12 mg/day on peripheral neuropathy grounds (EFSA NDA Panel, EFSA J 2023;21:e8006, PMID 37207271, DOI 10.2903/j.efsa.2023.8006). Not one case has been attributed to food B6.
items.form_caveat: This is a genuine case where the food is safe and the concentrated form is not, and the reason is dose plus kinetics rather than any exotic compound. Food B6 arrives as pyridoxal phosphate and pyridoxamine phosphate bound in the matrix, plus glycosylated pyridoxine in plant foods, released and absorbed gradually across a meal. A tablet delivers a bolus of free pyridoxine. The accepted mechanism for the neuropathy is that free pyridoxine at high concentration outruns conversion to pyridoxal 5-phosphate and acts at PLP-dependent sites in the dorsal root ganglion, which lack a blood-nerve barrier. Pyridoxal-5-phosphate supplements are marketed as the safe alternative on the strength of that mechanism, but the human evidence is thin and EFSA applies the 12 mg/day UL to total B6 regardless of form, so treating P5P as exempt is not supported. One practical consequence: because B6 is added to energy drinks, fortified cereals and B-complex products, people accumulate supplemental doses without intending to, and the UL is easy to cross by stacking products while eating a diet that contributes almost nothing to the risk.
items.bioavailability: Roughly 75% of dietary B6 is absorbed. Plant B6 is partly pyridoxine-5'-beta-D-glucoside, which is about half as available as free pyridoxine and can act as a weak antagonist: women fed a diet high in pyridoxine glucoside showed a measurable decline in B6 status indicators (J Nutr 1996, PMID 8857512). So plant-source B6 numbers overstate the delivered amount, and the gap between a plant food and a tablet is wider than the composition table suggests. Cooking removes more. USDA Table of Nutrient Retention Factors Release 6 (2007) gives B6 retention of 50% for roasted beef, 35% for beef braised or simmered without the drippings, 45% for liver simmered without drippings, 80% for roasted chicken, 50% for legumes boiled 2-2.5 h, 65% for legumes boiled 45-75 min and drained, and 85% for greens boiled in water to cover. A raw-basis figure such as the 0.933 mg/100 g for raw tuna is not what lands on the plate.

items.availability_note: Genuinely rich and cheap in ordinary food. A single medium red pepper or one guava exceeds the 90 mg adult RDA on its own, and a cup of strawberries or one medium orange comes close. This is the one ingredient in this set where a normal diet not only meets the requirement but can approach supplement territory. Synthetic ascorbic acid is manufactured (Reichstein or two-step fermentation from glucose), but it is the identical molecule, so the synthetic label carries no penalty here.

items.dose_gap: Unlike the other three, the supplement dose here is physically reachable by eating, which makes the honest answer more interesting than a flat impossibility. A 1,000 mg tablet equals 781 g of raw red pepper (about 6.6 medium peppers), or 439 g of guava (8 fruits), or 552 g of blackcurrants, or 1.70 kg of strawberries, or 1.88 kg of orange (14 medium oranges), or 2.0 litres of fresh orange juice. A 500 mg dose is 3.3 red peppers or 7 oranges. Eccentric, but not fantasy. The real gap is that the dose above about 200 mg is pointless rather than unreachable. Levine et al. gave 30-2,500 mg/day under depletion-repletion control: bioavailability was complete at a 200 mg single dose, fell off at 500 mg and above with the absorbed excess appearing in urine, leucocytes saturated at 100 mg/day and plasma at 1,000 mg/day (PNAS 1996;93:3704-9, PMID 8623000, DOI 10.1073/pnas.93.8.3704). So the honest framing is that four or five servings of ordinary fruit and vegetables reach the physiologically useful plateau, and the 1,000 mg tablet mostly funds expensive urine. The one number that should temper any composition table, though, is what survives handling: see cooking and storage below.
items.form_caveat: Effectively NONE on the molecule. Synthetic and food-derived vitamin C are chemically identical and all steady-state human comparative bioavailability studies show no difference; some acute pharmacokinetic studies show minor transient differences of no physiological consequence (Carr and Vissers, Nutrients 2013;5:4284-304, PMID 24169506, DOI 10.3390/nu5114284). This kills the 'natural vitamin C is better absorbed' claim, and it also means acerola, camu-camu and rose hip products carry no absorption advantage; most such products are in any case standardised by adding synthetic ascorbic acid, so the consumer is buying the synthetic molecule with fruit powder attached. What the whole food genuinely adds is the rest of the matrix, potassium, folate, carotenoids, flavonoids and fibre, none of which is in the tablet, and none of which the vitamin C evidence is actually about. Where a caveat does bite is the classic textbook recommendation. Spinach is the folklore answer for vitamins in green vegetables, but its vitamin C is modest at 28.1 mg/100 g, a realistic 30 g cup gives 8.4 mg, and boiling extracts most of what is there: in fresh-cut spinach, boiling moved 60% of the vitamin C and 50% of the flavonoids into the cooking water (Gil et al., J Agric Food Chem 1999, PMID 10794612). Recommending boiled spinach for vitamin C is close to recommending the cooking water.
items.bioavailability: Absorption is near-complete up to about 200 mg per dose via the sodium-dependent transporter SVCT1, declines above 500 mg, and the plateau is reached at 1,000 mg/day (PMID 8623000). Absorption is therefore not the variable that matters; retention before eating is. Cooking and storage losses, all from USDA Table of Nutrient Retention Factors Release 6 (2007), ascorbic acid column: greens boiled in water to cover and drained retain 55% (code 3005), greens boiled in a little water and drained 60% (code 3004), greens stir-fried 85% (code 3008), greens cooked from frozen and drained 60%; other vegetables boiled in water to cover and drained 75%, steamed 85%; potatoes baked in the skin 80%, boiled pared and drained 75%, and only 25% when boiled after storage and browned (code 3311); canned fruit 50% and dried fruit 20%. Steaming beats boiling and draining, consistently: in broccoli every method except steaming caused significant vitamin C loss (Yuan et al., J Zhejiang Univ Sci B 2009, PMID 19650196, DOI 10.1631/jzus.b0920051). Storage compounds it, since refrigerated storage of fruit and vegetables lowers vitamin C along with anthocyanins and total phenolics (PMID 28737734). Practical upshot: a week-old boiled vegetable can deliver a quarter of its table value, so the 27% loss between raw broccoli at 89.2 mg/100 g and boiled broccoli at 64.9 mg/100 g is the optimistic case, not the worst one.

misclassifications: Not a wrong tag, but an inconsistent convention: folic acid is tagged SYNTHETIC because the marketed molecule is manufactured, while 'High-dose vitamin B6' is tagged RICH even though the marketed object is 50-500 mg pyridoxine hydrochloride, a manufactured crystalline salt with no dietary counterpart at that dose. The submission's own note concedes this ('Food is a rich source of the vitamin and not a source of the dose'). Either the tag describes the nutrient (in which case folic acid's group should be labelled by folate, which is RICH) or it describes the product as sold (in which case high-dose pyridoxine is closer to SYNTHETIC). Pyridoxine itself does occur in food, so RICH is defensible for the molecule; the inconsistency is in what the field is measuring.

Vitamin B12 tagged RICH is correct for omnivores but the tag is population-dependent in a way the single word hides. For an unfortified plant-based diet the same evidence in the note makes B12 effectively absent: the only credible source is dried nori at 2.33 ug per 3 g sheet, from a product whose content varies about elevenfold by origin and degrades with toasting and storage. A reader taking RICH at face value gets the wrong answer for exactly the population that needs the right one.

Folic acid tagged SYNTHETIC survives challenge and should stand. I looked for a genuine dietary source and there is none: USDA's own component structure separates 'folic acid' from 'folate, food', and every food in FDC with non-zero folic acid is fortified or enriched (beef liver, lentils, spinach, chickpeas, asparagus and broccoli all read folic acid 0 and folate food = folate total). The three foods listed in the item are correctly identified as fortification vehicles.

Vitamin C tagged RICH survives challenge and is the strongest classification in the set: one 119 g red pepper (152 mg) or one 55 g guava (125 mg) exceeds the 90 mg RDA, verified against FDC. No trace-amount inflation anywhere in that food list.
missing_foods: Fortified ready-to-eat breakfast cereal is missing from the folic acid item, and it is the archetypal folic acid vehicle. US brands fortified to 100% DV carry 400 ug folic acid per serving, an entire periconceptional dose in one bowl, which is a stronger illustration of 'the only folic acid in the food supply is what fortification put there' than yeast extract, oatmeal and bread combined. Enriched pasta and enriched white rice, the mandated US enrichment vehicles, are also absent. Numbers are label-dependent and should be cited per product.

Chicken liver, all classes, cooked, simmered: 578 ug food folate/100 g (FDC 171061), more than twice the braised beef liver used in the folate dose gap. This omission is load-bearing, not cosmetic: 680 ug DFE needs only 118 g of chicken liver, under three 44 g livers, which is a plausible portion and materially weakens the 'technically reachable, practically not sustained' framing. Lamb liver, pan-fried, is 400 ug DFE/100 g (FDC 172533).

Sunflower seed kernels, dried: 227 ug DFE/100 g (FDC 170562), a folate source in the same class as the legumes listed, and 1.34 mg B6/100 g, which is richer per 100 g than the dry-roasted pistachios that head the B6 list. Raw garlic is 1.24 mg B6/100 g (FDC 169230).

Mollusks, mussel, blue, cooked, moist heat: 24.0 ug B12/100 g (FDC 174217). The submission used the raw entry and a retention factor instead of the cooked entry that USDA publishes, which halves the figure for the food people actually eat. Pacific oyster, raw is 16.0 ug/100 g (FDC 174219) and lamb liver, pan-fried is 85.7 ug/100 g (FDC 172533); the class the submission skips entirely (octopus, mackerel, herring, beef kidney, crab, caviar) all sit well above the salmon and milk rows that were included.

Fortified nutritional yeast and fortified plant milks and cereals are absent from the B12 food rows even though the item's own dose_gap concludes 'fortified foods or a tablet are the honest answer'. The one practical answer for the one population with a real gap never gets a row. Contents are label-dependent, which is the reason to name the category and cite the label rather than omit it.

Acerola, raw: 1,680 mg vitamin C/100 g (FDC 171686), roughly 81 mg from a single 4.8 g fruit. It appears in the vitamin C item only as something being debunked, never as the richest verified source in the database. Raw kale at 93.4 mg/100 g (FDC 168421) is also missing, which matters because the item spends a paragraph on spinach as the folklore green (28.1 mg, and boiling takes 60% of that) without naming the green that actually delivers. Rose hips, camu-camu, chilli peppers, papaya and Brussels sprouts round out the omitted set.
dose_gap_errors: Vitamin B12: '222 litres of whole milk' to reach 1,000 ug. The division is right but the unit is not. 1,000 / 0.0045 = 222,222 g, which is 222 kg of milk, and at a density of about 1.03 kg/L that is roughly 216 litres. Corrected figure: about 216 L (222 kg).

Vitamin C: '2.0 litres of fresh orange juice' for a 1,000 mg dose. Same unit slip. 1,000 / 0.50 = 2,000 g of juice, which at about 1.04 kg/L is roughly 1.9 litres. Corrected figure: about 1.9 L (2.0 kg).

Vitamin B12, mussels row: per_portion 10.2 ug and '425% of the 2.4 ug RDA' do not follow from the row's own stated basis. Applying the declared 90% steaming retention to the raw value gives 9.18 ug (383%); using the cooked USDA entry that should have been used gives 20.4 ug per 85 g (850%). Corrected figure: 20.4 ug, 850% of the RDA.

Vitamin B12 nori: 'a product whose content varies fourfold by origin'. The 4.1-fold ratio only holds inside the submission's own truncated 32.3-133.8 range. Against the cited paper's full spread (12.3 ug/100 g New Zealand karengo to 133.8 ug/100 g Korean laver) the variation is about elevenfold. Corrected figure: roughly elevenfold.

Vitamin B12 nori: 'about 4 g/day of dried purple laver, which is roughly one and a half sheets'. At the 3 g sheet weight used in the same item's food row, 4 g is 1.33 sheets. Corrected figure: about one and a third sheets.

Everything else recomputes. I re-ran all four dose_gap blocks line by line: 400 ug x 1.7 = 680 DFE and x 2.0 = 800 fasting; 376 g lentils, 219 g edamame, 269 g beef liver, 395 g chickpeas, 351 g spinach (11.7 thirty-gram cups), 456 g asparagus (30.4 spears), 630 g broccoli, and 4.7 kg lentils for 8,500 DFE; 1.01 kg clams, 1.42 kg liver, 11.2 kg sardines, 35.7 kg salmon; 100 mg B6 = 76.9x RDA, 8.93 kg pistachios, 9.80 kg liver, 10.7 kg tuna, 16.7 kg chicken, 27.2 kg banana = 231 bananas, 50 mg = 4.46 kg or 116 bananas, 12 mg UL = 1.07 kg pistachios or 3.27 kg banana (27.7 bananas); 1,000 mg vitamin C = 781 g red pepper (6.6), 439 g guava (8.0), 552 g blackcurrant, 1.70 kg strawberries, 1.88 kg orange (14.4), and 500 mg = 3.3 peppers or 7 oranges. All correct to the stated precision.
verification_report.net_assessment:
Unusually accurate submission. Of roughly 60 numeric food figures I could check against source, every per-100 g composition value and every portion gram weight matched USDA FoodData Central exactly, including details that are normally where fabrication shows up: the pistachio B6 data-point count (13) and analytical range (0.484-1.80), the separate folic acid and food folate components for the three fortified foods, the 92 g drained sardine can, the 86 g half breast, the 4-spear 60 g asparagus portion, and the split between raw (89.2 mg) and boiled (64.9 mg) broccoli. Every one of the 16 PMIDs I checked resolves to a real paper with the stated journal, year, volume and pages, and the quoted findings match the abstracts (266 ug/meal threshold, 83%/17% spirulina cobamides, eggs under 9% absorbed, IF saturation at 1.5-2.0 ug/meal, complete vitamin C bioavailability at 200 mg, 60% of spinach vitamin C into the cooking water, EFSA's 12 mg/day from a 50 mg reference point with UF 4). Roughly 30 retention factors from USDA Release 6 are all correct, verified row by row in the actual table. I found no invented sources.

Four things need fixing. The one substantive error is the mussels row: the submission used the raw entry (12.0 ug/100 g) plus a hand-applied retention factor, then failed to apply the factor anyway, when USDA publishes the cooked food at 24.0 ug/100 g. The correct row is 20.4 ug per 3 oz and 850% of the RDA, not 10.2 ug and 425%, and the general lesson is that a retention factor is the wrong tool when a cooked composition entry exists. Second, food folate in the yeast extract row is 793 ug, not 797. Third, two unit slips where grams were reported as litres (222 kg of milk is about 216 L; 2,000 g of juice is about 1.9 L). Fourth, three retention CODES are misattributed even though their values are right (stir-fried greens is 3015 not 3008, steamed in-shell shellfish is 2702 not 2770, roasted beef is 0601 not 1301) and the nori range floor is 12.3 ug/100 g in the cited paper, making the variation elevenfold rather than fourfold.

On classification: SYNTHETIC for folic acid and RICH for vitamin C both survive adversarial challenge cleanly. RICH for B12 is right for omnivores but hides a population-dependent reversal for unfortified plant diets. RICH for high-dose B6 is inconsistent with the convention that produced SYNTHETIC for folic acid, since the object being classified is a 50-500 mg manufactured salt. The most consequential omission is a substantive one rather than a decorative one: chicken liver at 578 ug food folate/100 g means 680 ug DFE takes 118 g of liver, which weakens the folate item's central rhetorical move about the food-folate route being impractical, and it should be addressed head-on rather than left out. Fortified breakfast cereal (400 ug folic acid per serving) and fortified nutritional yeast are missing from the two items whose conclusions depend on fortification being the honest answer.
